The Longest Saturday

Three people work in the same shopping centre. We asked them what they normally do — and what is happening right now, on the busiest Saturday of the year.

BAHODIR — bookshop. On a normal day I open at nine and there are three or four customers before eleven. I put new books on the shelves, I make coffee, and sometimes I read. Right now there is a queue to the door and I'm carrying boxes from the back room. I'm not reading anything today. My colleague is looking for a book called Quiet Mornings, which I find very funny.

MALIKA — café. I usually make about a hundred coffees a day. I know the regular customers and I know what they want before they say it. Today I'm making one every forty seconds and I don't know anybody. We aren't serving food after two o'clock, because the kitchen is too small for this. I started at eight this morning and I'm still standing on the same square metre of floor.

ELDOR — information desk. Normally people ask me where the chemist is, or where the cash machine is. It's a quiet job and I like it. Today they are asking me where their children are. Four so far, and it is only one o'clock. We find them near the ice cream, always. Right now a man is asking me why the car park is full, and I'm trying not to laugh.

So is the busiest day the worst day? Bahodir says yes. Malika says yes, but the tips are better. Eldor says no — the quiet days are longer.

Grammar · present continuous, and which tense to use

TUSHUNTIRISH — SHAKLI

Present continuous = am / is / are + feʼl + -ing. U hozir boʻlayotgan narsalar uchun.

+ Tasdiq. I'm reading a magazine. · We're waiting at the entrance. · She's talking on the phone.

− Inkor. I'm not drinking coffee. · We aren't / We're not waiting. · He isn't / He's not coming.

? Soʻroq. Are you parking the car? · Is he buying anything? · What are you doing?

→ Qisqa javoblar. Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. · Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. · Yes, we are. / No, we aren't.

be ni hech qachon tushirib qoldirmang. ✗ I working today → ✓ I'm working today. Yolgʻiz -ing feʼl emas.

Imlo qoidasi

Feʼl

-ing shakli

koʻp feʼllar — shunchaki -ing qoʻshiladi

wait · look · buy

waiting · looking · buying

-e bilan tugasa — e tushib qoladi

write · come · make

writing · coming · making

bitta unli + bitta undosh — undosh ikkilanadi

swim · run · shop · get

swimming · running · shopping · getting

-y bilan tugasa — hech narsa oʻzgarmaydi

study · buy · carry

studying · buying · carrying

DIQQAT — IMLO

Oʻqituvchingiz eng koʻp koʻradigan toʻrttasi:

✗ writting → ✓ writing · ✗ comeing / comming → ✓ coming · ✗ studing → ✓ studying · ✗ swiming → ✓ swimming

Qoida: oxirgi -e tushib qoladi, oxirgi undosh faqat bitta unlidan keyin ikkilanadi, oxirgi -y ga esa tegilmaydi. Shuning uchun write da e yoʻqoladi, swim da m ikkilanadi, study esa hammasini saqlaydi.

TUSHUNTIRISH — QAYSI ZAMON?

Ikkala zamon ham hozirgi vaqt haqida, shuning uchun savol doim bitta: odatdami yoki hozirmi?

Present simple = odatda qiladigan ishlarimiz. I open at nine. · People ask me where the chemist is. · She wears jeans.

Present continuous = hozir boʻlayotgan narsalar. I'm carrying boxes. · A man is asking me about the car park. · She's wearing a dress.

Qaysi biri ekanini vaqt soʻzlari aytadi:

simple — always · usually · normally · often · sometimes · never · every day · at weekends

continuous — now · right now · today · at the moment · this week

DIQQAT — NOTOʻGʻRI ZAMON

1 Simple kerak joyda continuous. ✗ All the masks are being really beautiful. → ✓ All the masks are really beautiful. Niqoblar faqat bugun chiroyli emas.

2 Continuous kerak joyda simple. ✗ Look — I stand in the middle of the square. → ✓ I'm standing in the middle of the square. U yerda doim turmaydi.

3 Mos kelmaydigan vaqt soʻzi. ✗ I'm going to school every day. → ✓ I go to school every day.

TWO FESTIVALS, TWO SETS OF CLOTHES

Feria de Abril, Seville (Spain). Six days, usually two weeks after Easter. The fair is a field of striped tents called casetas, with dancing inside. Many women wear the traje de flamenca — a long dress with big flowers or spots and rows of frills. At midday, hundreds of horses and carriages come through.

Gion Matsuri, Kyoto (Japan). The whole of July, with the big float parade on 17 July. The floats, called yamaboko, can be 25 metres tall and weigh 12 tonnes. On the three evenings before, the streets close to traffic and fill with food stalls. People wear the yukata, a light cotton summer kimono, with wooden sandals.
